transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-09 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Laura (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SRE), Marcus (Peregrine), Anita (Plat Eng), Samuel (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): post-incident tech review; root cause appears to be aggressive watermarking combined with synchronous spillback to on-prem disk; prefix hotspots amplified eviction churn and caused long-tail latency; discussed mitigations including per-prefix throttles, async snapshotting, and telemetry improvements.

Topics: KV watermark thresholds, spillback behavior, eviction scoring, snapshotting, prefix reuse, batching interplay, on-prem disk I/O constraints.

00:00:05 - Laura: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for squeezing this in. I know we hit that 3am page alert on Friday, so wanted to run through the end-to-end and make sure we have clear next steps. Marcus, can you give the timeline from your side?
00:00:20 - Marcus: Yeah, sure, uh so Friday at 02:42 we saw token latency shoot up to the 8 to 12 second range, some tails even higher. The app started seeing timeouts, and our logs show repeated KV miss spikes followed by disk reads.
00:00:38 - Anita: I just want to flag, we were doing a rollout of a new prefix mapping that day but it was a small release, not expected to create hotspots.
00:00:46 - Diego: When you say disk reads, is that on the on-prem local NVMe, or to a network filestore?
00:00:52 - Marcus: Local NVMe—it's our private deployment with Redwood Private. The KV runtime spilled entries to disk after hitting watermarks.
00:01:03 - Priya: Right, and the spill mechanism today is synchronous by default for safety—so writes block until snapshot completes, which protects correctness but can amplify latency.
00:01:15 - Samuel: Could you explain the watermarking logic again? I thought Redwood used a two-tier watermark?
00:01:22 - Diego: Yeah, quick recap: we have low and high watermarks per node. When the node crosses low, it starts background snapshotting and more aggressive prefetch rules. When it crosses high, it attempts to spill the least-recently-used segments to disk and may start rejecting new prefetched prefixes depending on config. But for this customer the spill path went sync because of the way the on-prem config was set.
00:01:48 - Marcus: I think the big issue was a noisy prefix—one client job iterated a few hundred unique long contexts and reused the same prefix id over and over which kept it artificially "hot". That caused eviction churn because the KV store kept pinning and evicting nearby entries.
00:02:05 - Anita: There's also the prefix reuse pattern—our app reuses short prefix tokens as anchors and that inflated the prefix frequency counter.
00:02:12 - Laura: This is where we should talk about per-prefix quotas and decaying counters. Diego, you mentioned an LFU/LRU hybrid in pre-work?
00:02:21 - Diego: Yeah, the hybrid idea is to combine recency and frequency: we keep an approximate frequency counter per prefix with exponential decay (so hot suddenly decays if no recent hits), and we combine that with an LRU score to decide eviction priority. That reduces thrashing from a looped job that touches many contexts briefly.
00:02:40 - Marcus: Does the frequency counter add a lot of memory overhead? We're memory constrained on the nodes.
00:02:47 - Diego: We use a compact sketch—like a tiny count-min with decay—so the overhead per prefix is small (tens of bytes). But if you have tens of millions of prefixes it adds up; that's why we also want per-tenant caps.
00:03:01 - Samuel: What about snapshotting frequency, can we move to async-only for on-prem?
00:03:07 - Priya: Async snapshotting reduces tail latency because the write is queued and doesn't block the critical path, but it increases the window of discrepancy on failover. For Private deployments we give admins the option—safety vs latency tradeoff. In your case the default was conservative and ended up blocking.
00:03:26 - Anita: Is there a middle ground? like bounded sync (sync up to N MB then async)?
00:03:31 - Diego: Yep, bounded sync is an option—do synchronous snapshots for small batches and switch to async once the batch grows. Also chunked snapshots so you don't block on a single huge write.
00:03:44 - 00:04:00 - (soft cross-talk, background typing)
00:04:01 - Laura: Let's dig into telemetry. Marcus, can you confirm what you saw in the KV metrics?
00:04:06 - Marcus: We saw eviction rate spike, cache hit ratio drop from 0.93 to 0.67, and disk read latency average went from 1ms to 7ms under load. The node watermark metric flipped to high for about 12 minutes across three nodes.
00:04:20 - Diego: Do you have per-prefix histograms? The aggregated hit ratio can mask hot prefixes.
00:04:26 - Marcus: We do but we didn't ship them to Redwood yet. We'll pull the top 100 prefixes.
00:04:32 - Priya: Also, we noticed IO saturation on the NVMe—lots of small random reads. If the KV spill format is not optimized for small random access it will amplify latency.
00:04:44 - Samuel: What format do you use when spilling? Is it a log-structured file or block store?
00:04:49 - Diego: Currently spill uses a compact binary segment store optimized for sequential writes and small random reads, but there are cases where access patterns devolve into many tiny reads which are painful on some consumer-grade NVMe. For on-prem we recommend enterprise SSDs and slightly larger spill chunk sizes.
00:05:06 - Anita: Our infra uses mid-range datacenter NVMe—should we change hardware or config first?
00:05:13 - Priya: Try config first: increase prefetch window to reduce small random reads, enable compressed spill format to reduce IO, and tune the io_scheduler to batch operations. Hardware upgrade helps but is more expensive.
00:05:25 - 00:05:40 - (brief pause)
00:05:41 - Marcus: On the subject of batching, we've noticed that heavy request batching increases KV pressure because more tokens are generated per request and our KV warmup isn't keeping up. Any suggestions?
00:05:53 - Diego: For bursty batching, you want adaptive batch sizing that considers current KV hit ratio and queue depth. Also consider pre-warming common prefixes in the request pipeline. Redwood has a prefetch policy you can tune to be more aggressive for steady-state traffic, less aggressive for bursts.
00:06:10 - Laura: One recurring ask from customers is better visibility into prefix-level eviction and a way to pin critical prefixes. Is pinning on the roadmap?
00:06:19 - Diego: Pinning is supported as a soft pin today—items can be scored to avoid eviction unless absolutely necessary. Hard pinning (never evict) has availability risks for multi-tenant clusters but we can expose per-namespace reserved memory quotas.
00:06:34 - Anita: If we reserve memory for our critical prefixes, can that be dynamic? Our traffic patterns change a lot during batch jobs.
00:06:40 - Diego: We can make reservations dynamic: time-bounded reservations that expire, or reservation based on business priority. That requires slightly more orchestration but doable.
00:06:50 - Samuel: Any thoughts about quantized KV entries? We were experimenting with 8-bit quantized key blobs to save space.
00:06:57 - Priya: Quantization for KV payloads helps memory but can slow deserialization slightly. It also complicates partial updates and diffs for snapshotting. If you go quantized, prefer a format that supports zero-copy reads so you don't pay decode penalties on the hot path.
00:07:15 - Marcus: Okay, concrete requests: we will send the top prefixes and logs, and we'd like Redwood to propose a config diff.
00:07:21 - Laura: We'll do that; Diego will draft the diff with the hybrid eviction, bounded sync snapshotting, and per-prefix caps.
00:07:28 - 00:07:50 - (brief housekeeping, switching to root cause timeline)
00:07:51 - Diego: From our perspective the incident chain was: noisy prefix pattern -> eviction churn -> synchronous spillback -> disk IO saturation -> longer latencies -> ripple across request queue -> timeouts. Two amplifiers were the conservative on-prem snapshotting and the lack of per-prefix backpressure.
00:08:08 - Marcus: That matches our traces. We also saw jitter in the KV background compaction job which ran concurrently and contended for the same IO. That was unfortunate timing.
00:08:20 - Anita: Is compaction scheduled or adaptive?
00:08:24 - Diego: It's adaptive, but you can pin it to low-priority cgroups or tune thresholds so it doesn't run during peak windows. For Private deployments we recommend off-peak compaction.
00:08:36 - Laura: Let's talk about instrumentation changes. We propose adding these new metrics: per-prefix hit ratio (top N), eviction-streaks (count of repeated evictions for a prefix), async-snapshot-queue-length, and disk-io-wait.
00:08:54 - Marcus: Those look good. We'll need them in Prometheus format or as a CSV dump.
00:08:59 - Diego: We can ship a Prom exporter module. It will add low overhead if you sample top prefixes only.
00:09:07 - 00:09:35 - (short stretch)
00:09:36 - Samuel: I have a question about multi-node routing. If one node spills, can requests be routed away to nodes with warmer caches?
00:09:44 - Diego: Smart routing can do that: route requests by prefix affinity so that warm prefixes map to nodes that already hold them. But in highly dynamic environments prefix shuffling can create hot-cold transitions. As an alternative, fallbacks can call a faster hosted variant if latency exceeds threshold.
00:09:59 - Marcus: For us, network egress is expensive so cross-node hops are undesirable.
00:10:05 - Priya: Then per-node isolation and per-prefix quotas become more important. We should avoid cross-node fallback unless necessary.
00:10:12 - Anita: Any immediate config we should flip?
00:10:15 - Diego: Short list: turn on per-prefix caps (soft limit 2x baseline), enable bounded sync snapshotting, increase spill chunk size to 256KB, and enable compressed spill format. We'll provide a diff.
00:10:28 - Laura: We'll include those in the email.
00:10:31 - 00:10:55 - (discussion continues on load tests and acceptance criteria)
00:10:56 - Marcus: For acceptance, we want 99.9th percentile token latency under synthetic 2x peak for 48 hours with no node crossing high watermark.
00:11:08 - Diego: Agreed. We'll also instrument eviction-streaks and give you a threshold alert rule.
00:11:14 - Anita: One last on VPC/network: do we see higher latency when the control plane is multi-region?
00:11:20 - Priya: Control plane chatter can add small overhead to metadata ops, but the heavy path is local. For on-prem you can pin control plane egress to a regional endpoint or run a private control plane bundle.
00:11:33 - Samuel: We might consider moving to a private control plane in our DC. What's the lift?
00:11:37 - Laura: It's possible; we can scope the Private deployment options. Diego, maybe we triage before the next call.
00:11:44 - Diego: Yup, I'll add an item.
00:11:48 - 00:12:05 - (wrap up)
00:12:06 - Laura: Recap: Redwood to send config diff and Prom exporter; Peregrine to share prefix heatmap and run 48h test; follow up meeting in two weeks. Any final Qs?
00:12:19 - Marcus: No, thanks all.
00:12:21 - Anita: Thanks.
00:12:23 - Samuel: Appreciate it.
